You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

notes.about: This page completes a restricted-use vaccination voucher example, explains Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), and introduces Project Nexus and participating national fast payment systems.
key_questions: Who pays MDR, who shares it, and how does it affect the merchant's receipt?
Who leads Project Nexus, what does it connect, and why is a standardized connection useful?
Which countries and fast payment systems are paired in the table?

decisions.decision: Combine the repeated Project Nexus bullets into their corresponding teaching items while covering both sets of blocks.
decisions.reason: The lower bullets repeat the same claims; they do not add distinct content.

decisions.decision: Treat Merchant Discount Rate as a heading rather than a facts-and-numbers claim.

output.page_summary: A vaccination voucher is restricted to its designated purpose. MDR is paid by the merchant and shared across payment-system participants; a ₹1,000 sale at 2% MDR leaves ₹980 for the merchant. Project Nexus, led by the BIS Innovation Hub, aims to link national fast payment systems through a standardized connection and simplify cross-border transfers.

items.content: You can redeem it only for vaccination at an authorized center—not withdraw cash or spend it elsewhere.

teacher_understanding.question: What can the voucher in the continued example be used for?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its permitted use is vaccination at an authorized center. Cash withdrawal and spending elsewhere are excluded.

teacher_understanding.question: Which words establish both purpose and place restrictions?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Only for vaccination' specifies the purpose, while 'at an authorized center' specifies the permitted place of redemption.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this differ from receiving unrestricted cash?
teacher_understanding.answer: A purpose-restricted voucher directs purchasing power toward a specified service, whereas unrestricted cash can generally be spent across many purposes.

prerequisites: A voucher as a claim to a specified benefit
items.exam_note: Distinguish purpose-specific redemption from cash transfer; do not infer the instrument's name from this page alone.

Restricting redemption prevents treating the voucher as freely spendable cash.

unpack.consequence: A voucher's stated value does not imply a right to withdraw that value as cash.

items.content: Merchant Discount Rate
items.type_note: This is a section heading, not a numerical claim despite the word 'Rate'.
items.exam_note: Introduces payment-system charges.

items.content: MDR is the fees that a merchant must pay to his (acquirer) bank for every card transaction.

teacher_understanding.question: What does MDR mean in a card payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the transaction fee payable by the merchant to the acquiring bank, rather than the amount paid for the goods themselves.

teacher_understanding.question: What identifies the payer, recipient, and occasion for MDR?
teacher_understanding.answer: The definition names the merchant as payer, the acquirer bank as recipient, and each card transaction as the occasion.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a merchant receive less than the customer's purchase amount?
teacher_understanding.answer: Payment acceptance involves services supplied by payment participants; a transaction fee can be deducted from the sale proceeds before the merchant receives the net amount.

prerequisites: A bank account receiving sale proceeds
items.exam_note: Core definition; 'discount' here is not a shopping discount given to the customer.

terms.plain_meaning: card payment लेने पर दुकानदार से लगने वाली fee
terms.everyday_image: दुकान की पूरी बिक्री में से payment की fee कटना

terms.plain_meaning: दुकानदार की तरफ card payment लेने वाला bank
terms.everyday_image: दुकान के payment counter के पीछे काम करने वाला bank

why_chain.step: The merchant needs a way to accept a customer's card payment.
The book identifies MDR as the merchant's fee for that transaction.

unpack.example_or_place: A shop accepting a card payment; the diagram below uses ₹1,000.
unpack.consequence: Gross purchase value and the merchant's net receipt can differ.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate the sale amount from the payment-processing fee.
unpack.level_extra: Do not interpret 'discount' as a customer concession or assume the illustrated 2% is universal.

items.content:
The merchant does not pay the entire MDR to one entity. It is shared among:
Acquiring Bank (merchant's bank)
Issuing Bank (customer's bank)
Card Network (RuPay, Visa, Mastercard, etc.)
Payment Service Provider/Gateway, where applicable

teacher_understanding.question: Which participants share MDR?
teacher_understanding.answer: The acquiring bank, issuing bank, card network, and, where applicable, payment service provider or gateway share it. The merchant's payment to the acquirer does not mean the acquirer keeps the whole fee.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the acquiring and issuing banks situated in the transaction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The acquiring bank is on the merchant's side; the issuing bank is the customer's bank. RuPay, Visa, and Mastercard are listed separately as card networks.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these roles differ in a typical card payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: The acquirer supports merchant acceptance, the issuer supplies and authorizes the customer's card facility, the network carries transaction messages between participants, and a gateway can provide the connection through which payment information is submitted.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the phrase 'where applicable' be retained?
teacher_understanding.answer: The list makes the provider or gateway's inclusion conditional rather than saying that this participant receives a share in every transaction.

items.exam_note: Distinguish issuer from acquirer and networks from banks. No percentage allocation among participants is given.

terms.everyday_image: दुकान की रकम पाने वाली तरफ का bank

why_chain.step: A card payment needs coordination between the customer's and merchant's sides.
MDR is shared across the participants named in the book rather than retained entirely by one entity.

unpack.example_or_place: RuPay, Visa, and Mastercard are the page's examples of card networks.
unpack.consequence: The initial fee recipient and the final fee beneficiaries are not necessarily identical.
unpack.visual_verb: Split one fee into participant shares without inventing share sizes.
unpack.level_extra: Useful for matching and correct-statement questions; 'shared' does not mean 'equally shared'.

items.content: The merchant pays MDR, not the customer.

teacher_understanding.question: Who bears the MDR charge as stated here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The merchant is the identified payer of MDR; the customer is not identified as its payer.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the diagram support this statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The customer pays ₹1,000, but the merchant receives ₹980 at 2% MDR, locating the deduction on the merchant's receipt.

teacher_understanding.question: Why distinguish the purchase payment from MDR?
teacher_understanding.answer: Paying for goods and paying a payment-acceptance fee are different obligations. The customer's purchase amount should not be confused with the merchant's processing charge.

items.exam_note: Direct payer-identification trap. Do not extend this statement into a claim about all indirect pricing effects.

terms.plain_meaning: सामान या सेवा बेचकर payment लेने वाला
terms.everyday_image: card machine पर आपकी खरीदारी का payment लेने वाला दुकानदार

why_chain.step: A customer pays the purchase amount.
The MDR deduction reduces the merchant's receipt in the illustration.

unpack.example_or_place: ₹1,000 paid by the customer versus ₹980 received by the merchant.
unpack.consequence: Identify the fee payer separately from the buyer.
unpack.visual_verb: Deduct the fee from the merchant's side.
unpack.level_extra: Contractual fee payer is the issue here, not a full analysis of economic incidence.

items.content: A left-to-right flow connects Customer → Merchant → Banks & [and] Payment Network. The first arrow says 'Pays ₹1,000'; the second says 'MDR shared'. Beneath the flow: 'Merchant receives ₹980 when MDR = 2%'. The fee is therefore ₹20 in this example.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the payment flow illustrate?
teacher_understanding.answer: It follows a ₹1,000 customer payment to the merchant and shows MDR being shared with banks and the payment network, leaving ₹980 for the merchant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which amounts are gross payment and net merchant receipt?
teacher_understanding.answer: ₹1,000 is the customer's gross purchase payment; ₹980 is the merchant's receipt at the illustrated 2% MDR.

teacher_understanding.question: How is the ₹20 difference calculated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Two percent means 2 per 100: ₹1,000 × 2/100 = ₹20. Subtracting ₹20 from ₹1,000 gives ₹980.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the arrows not be read as the complete banking settlement procedure?
teacher_understanding.answer: This is a simplified allocation picture. It identifies who pays and who shares the fee rather than showing every authorization, clearing, and settlement step.

items.exam_note: Illustrative calculation, not a claim that MDR is universally 2%.

At the illustrated rate, the deduction leaves the merchant ₹980.

unpack.consequence: The ₹20 gap represents the fee, not an unpaid part of the customer's bill.
unpack.visual_verb: Move ₹1,000, separate ₹20, and leave ₹980.
unpack.level_extra: ₹ denotes Indian rupees; % means per hundred; MDR = 2% specifies the illustrative rate.

teacher_understanding.question: What amount does this arrow represent?
teacher_understanding.answer: It represents a purchase payment of one thousand Indian rupees.

teacher_understanding.question: Which participants does it connect?
teacher_understanding.answer: It runs from Customer to Merchant, not from Merchant to the banking participants.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this amount used in the fee calculation?

teacher_understanding.answer: The full customer payment is shown on the incoming side, while the caption gives the merchant's lower net receipt after the fee.

items.exam_note: Central role is merchant, not issuing bank.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the outgoing arrow represent?
teacher_understanding.answer: It represents sharing of the MDR fee with payment participants, not transfer of the whole purchase value as a fee.

teacher_understanding.question: Which destination receives this arrow?
teacher_understanding.answer: The destination is the combined box for banks and the payment network.

teacher_understanding.question: How much is available for sharing in the illustrated transaction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fee pool is ₹20, calculated as 2% of ₹1,000; the page does not specify individual shares.

teacher_understanding.answer: It groups banks and the payment network as recipients of MDR shares.

teacher_understanding.answer: It distinguishes the merchant's acquiring bank from the customer's issuing bank.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should this box not be interpreted as one institution?
teacher_understanding.answer: The surrounding list explicitly distributes MDR among different kinds of participants; the box compresses those recipients for a simple diagram.

teacher_understanding.question: What relationship does the caption state?
teacher_understanding.answer: For the ₹1,000 payment shown, a 2% MDR leaves the merchant with ₹980.

teacher_understanding.question: Which symbols and units need interpretation?
teacher_understanding.answer: ₹ marks Indian rupees, '=' means equals, and '%' means per hundred; MDR is the fee rate in this caption.

A 2% deduction is ₹20, leaving ₹980.

items.content: Project Nexus
items.exam_note: Introduces cross-border payment-system connectivity.

items.where_on_page: first Project Nexus bullet and its lower repetition
items.content:
It is a multilateral cross-border payments initiative led by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub that aims to connect the fast payment systems (FPS) of different countries,
[The same bullet is printed again in the lower section.]

teacher_understanding.question: What is Project Nexus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is an initiative for connecting fast payment systems across countries through multilateral cooperation, led by the BIS Innovation Hub.

teacher_understanding.question: What establishes its leadership and international scope?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page explicitly names the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub and says it aims to connect FPS of different countries.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'multilateral cross-border' be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Multilateral' means involving several countries rather than just a pair. 'Cross-border' refers to payments between countries rather than within one country.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the project connect systems rather than merely name payment apps?
teacher_understanding.answer: Domestic payment systems already serve their own users; interoperability creates a way for payments to move between those national arrangements.

prerequisites: A payment system connecting payers and payees
items.exam_note: Leadership, multilateral character, and connection of FPS are key correct-statement facts.

terms.plain_meaning: कई देशों का साथ मिलकर काम करना
terms.everyday_image: दो लोगों की अलग बात के बजाय कई लोगों की एक साझा बैठक

terms.plain_meaning: एक देश से दूसरे देश में पैसा भेजना
terms.everyday_image: विदेश में रहने वाला व्यक्ति घर पैसे भेजे

terms.everyday_image: UPI से पैसा भेजने पर जल्दी पहुँच जाना

why_chain.step: People need to make payments beyond their own country's payment system.
Project Nexus aims to connect the FPS of different countries.

unpack.example_or_place: The adjoining table pairs India's UPI with other countries' fast payment systems.
unpack.consequence: Domestic fast-payment capabilities can become part of cross-border connectivity.
unpack.visual_verb: Connect separate national payment-system circles.
unpack.level_extra: BIS Innovation Hub is the named leader; do not replace it with a domestic payment authority.

items.where_on_page: Project Nexus objective bullet and its lower repetition
items.content:
Objective: Allowing people to send money internationally as easily as making a domestic UPI payment.
[Printed twice on this page.]

teacher_understanding.question: What familiar activity is used as the benchmark for international transfers?
teacher_understanding.answer: The book uses the ease of making a domestic UPI payment as the desired benchmark for sending money internationally.

teacher_understanding.question: What remains different between the two kinds of payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: A domestic payment stays within one country's setting; an international payment must work across national payment arrangements.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this objective relate to the project's design?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page's standardized connection between national instant payment systems is the proposed way to simplify international money transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this an objective rather than proof of identical service conditions?
teacher_understanding.answer: The wording describes the ease the project seeks to achieve; it does not supply measured transfer times, costs, or an assurance that all international transfers already match domestic UPI.

items.exam_note: Distinguish stated aim from proven universal availability, speed, or zero cost.

terms.plain_meaning: देश के अंदर UPI से payment करना
terms.everyday_image: दुकान का QR scan करके पैसे देना

why_chain.step: The book describes overseas transfers as involving fees and delays.
Nexus seeks an experience as easy as domestic UPI.

unpack.example_or_place: Compare a local UPI payment with sending money to someone in another country.
unpack.consequence: User convenience is the goal; system interconnection is the means.
unpack.visual_verb: Place a domestic payment and an international transfer side by side, then simplify the latter.
unpack.level_extra: An objective is not a guarantee of identical fees or instant completion in every case.

items.where_on_page: Project Nexus, UPI participation bullet and its lower repetition
items.content:
India's UPI is one of the founding payment systems participating in this project.
[Printed twice on this page.]

teacher_understanding.question: What role does the page assign to India's UPI?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies UPI as one of the founding payment systems participating in Project Nexus.

teacher_understanding.question: What supports identifying UPI with India?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bullet says 'India's UPI', and the country table pairs India with UPI.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does founding participation not mean that UPI leads Project Nexus?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page separately identifies the BIS Innovation Hub as the initiative's leader. UPI's stated role is that of a participating payment system.

items.exam_note: Participation and leadership are distinct; retain the book's founding-system wording without adding a date.

terms.plain_meaning: शुरुआत से जुड़ी payment व्यवस्थाएँ
terms.everyday_image: किसी साझा काम की शुरुआती टीम का हिस्सा होना

why_chain.step: Nexus needs national payment systems to participate.
The book identifies India's UPI as one of its founding systems.

unpack.example_or_place: India — UPI in the adjoining table.
unpack.consequence: India has a participating system; that does not make UPI the project leader.
unpack.visual_verb: Attach India's UPI node to the Nexus connection.
unpack.level_extra: A likely trap substitutes a participating system for the leading institution.

items.where_on_page: Project Nexus, existing-transfer problem bullet and its lower repetition
items.content:
Today, sending money abroad usually involves multiple correspondent banks, higher fees, and delays.
[Printed twice on this page.]

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page present a need for simpler cross-border payments?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes the usual overseas-transfer arrangement as involving several correspondent banks, higher fees, and delays.

teacher_understanding.question: How can correspondent banks make a transfer possible?
teacher_understanding.answer: When the sending and receiving banks do not have a direct arrangement, other banks can provide intermediate account and payment relationships through which the transfer is routed.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can extra intermediaries add time and cost?
teacher_understanding.answer: Additional institutions can introduce processing steps, checks, and charges. This explains the problem without claiming every overseas transfer follows the same route.

teacher_understanding.question: Does 'usually' mean all international payments necessarily use many banks?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. The page describes a common pattern rather than an exceptionless rule.

items.exam_note: Understand the problem Nexus addresses; retain the qualifier 'usually'.

terms.plain_meaning: दूसरे banks की तरफ से बीच में payment पहुँचाने में मदद करने वाले banks
terms.everyday_image: सीधा रास्ता न हो तो कई पड़ावों से सामान भेजना

why_chain.step: Money must reach a recipient through banks in another country.
Intermediate routing can add processing and charges, helping explain the fees and delays described.

unpack.example_or_place: A person sending money to family abroad.
unpack.consequence: Creates the motivation for a simpler standardized interconnection.
unpack.visual_verb: Route a transfer through several bank stops and show time and fee markers.
unpack.level_extra: Do not read 'usually' as 'always'; no fee amount or delay duration is provided.

items.where_on_page: below the country table, standardized connection bullet
items.content: Project Nexus creates a single standardized connection between national instant payment systems, so countries do not need to build separate payment links with every other country.

teacher_understanding.question: How does Nexus change the connection problem?
teacher_understanding.answer: A standardized connection between national instant payment systems replaces the need for each country to construct separate links with every other country.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a shared connection approach useful?
teacher_understanding.answer: Without common arrangements, each additional bilateral link may require separate technical coordination. A common connection model reduces repeated integration work.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'single standardized connection' be understood without overreading it?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means a common way of connecting systems, like using an agreed interface, rather than proof that countries abolish their own domestic systems.

teacher_understanding.question: What practical consequence does the page explicitly state?
teacher_understanding.answer: Countries no longer need to build a separate payment link with every other country for this connectivity model.

items.exam_note: Central design logic: multilateral standardized connectivity versus repeated country-to-country links.

terms.plain_meaning: एक तय साझा तरीके से जुड़ना, हर देश के लिए अलग जोड़ न बनाना
terms.everyday_image: हर device के लिए अलग plug के बजाय एक साझा socket का नियम

why_chain.step: Separate links with every other country create repeated connection work.
Nexus supplies a standardized connection so those separate links are not needed.

unpack.example_or_place: National systems such as UPI and PayNow shown as separate nodes joined through a common connection model.
unpack.consequence: Interconnection is simplified while the named national systems remain distinct.
unpack.visual_verb: Replace a web of pairwise lines with connections following one common standard.
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer a single currency, replacement of domestic systems, or detailed technical architecture.

items.where_on_page: right side of Project Nexus section, black table
items.content: Columns: Country | Fast Payment System. Rows, in order: India | UPI; Singapore | PayNow; Malaysia | DuitNow; Philippines | InstaPay; Thailand | PromptPay.
items.exam_note: Country-system matching table; all five pairings are preserved in child rows.

items.content: Country: India | Fast Payment System: UPI

teacher_understanding.question: Which fast payment system is paired with India?
teacher_understanding.answer: India is paired with UPI, also named in the text as a founding participating system.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this pairing established?
teacher_understanding.answer: The first data row places India in the Country column and UPI in the Fast Payment System column.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this row help explain Project Nexus?
teacher_understanding.answer: It supplies India's national-system example for the broader aim of connecting different countries' fast payment systems.

items.exam_note: Match India with UPI; distinguish system participation from BIS leadership.

terms.plain_meaning: भारत में जल्दी digital payment करने की व्यवस्था
terms.everyday_image: दुकान का QR scan करके पैसे देना

unpack.example_or_place: India.
unpack.consequence: Anchors the foreign-system names to a familiar Indian example.
unpack.visual_verb: Pair India with UPI.
unpack.level_extra: A table match establishes country association, not the detailed rules for every transfer.

items.content: Country: Singapore | Fast Payment System: PayNow

teacher_understanding.question: Which system is paired with Singapore?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table identifies PayNow as Singapore's fast payment system.

teacher_understanding.question: What fixes this country-system association?
teacher_understanding.answer: Singapore and PayNow occupy the same second data row under the two column headings.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this example fit the need for interconnection?
teacher_understanding.answer: A national system serves its own setting; linking systems across countries requires arrangements that let their payment information work together.

items.exam_note: Matching question: Singapore — PayNow.

terms.plain_meaning: इस table में Singapore की fast payment व्यवस्था का नाम
terms.everyday_image: भारत के UPI वाले खाने के सामने Singapore के लिए PayNow का नाम-पट्ट

unpack.example_or_place: Singapore.
unpack.consequence: Keep PayNow separate from Thailand's PromptPay and the other named systems.
unpack.visual_verb: Join Singapore and PayNow with one matching line.
unpack.level_extra: The table supplies the association, not specific fees or operational coverage.

items.content: Country: Malaysia | Fast Payment System: DuitNow

teacher_understanding.question: Which fast payment system belongs with Malaysia in this table?
teacher_understanding.answer: Malaysia is paired with DuitNow.

teacher_understanding.question: Which row provides the evidence?
teacher_understanding.answer: The third data row puts Malaysia under Country and DuitNow under Fast Payment System.

teacher_understanding.question: Why keep the system name distinct from the shared connection?
teacher_understanding.answer: The national system and the interconnection arrangement perform different roles: a common link connects systems rather than turning their names into one domestic service.

prerequisites: Project Nexus as an interconnection initiative
items.exam_note: Matching question: Malaysia — DuitNow.

terms.plain_meaning: इस table में Malaysia की fast payment व्यवस्था का नाम

unpack.example_or_place: Malaysia.
unpack.consequence: Avoid swapping DuitNow with Singapore's PayNow.
unpack.visual_verb: Pair Malaysia with DuitNow.

items.content: Country: Philippines | Fast Payment System: InstaPay

teacher_understanding.question: Which country is paired with InstaPay?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table pairs InstaPay with the Philippines.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this pairing shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fourth data row places Philippines and InstaPay alongside one another under the country and system headings.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the row reinforce the project's multilateral character?
teacher_understanding.answer: It adds another national-system example to the set of different countries shown beside the explanation of connecting their fast payment systems.

items.exam_note: Matching question: Philippines — InstaPay.

terms.plain_meaning: इस table में Philippines की fast payment व्यवस्था का नाम
terms.everyday_image: देश और उसकी payment सेवा को जोड़ने वाला नाम-पट्ट

unpack.example_or_place: Philippines.
unpack.consequence: A name suggesting speed does not by itself establish a specific transfer time.
unpack.visual_verb: Pair Philippines with InstaPay.
unpack.level_extra: Retain the capitalization InstaPay; the page gives no numerical speed claim.

items.content: Country: Thailand | Fast Payment System: PromptPay

teacher_understanding.question: Which system is paired with Thailand?
teacher_understanding.answer: Thailand is paired with PromptPay.

teacher_understanding.question: What confirms this association?
teacher_understanding.answer: The final data row lists Thailand in the Country column and PromptPay in the Fast Payment System column.

teacher_understanding.question: How should PromptPay be distinguished from PayNow?
teacher_understanding.answer: Use their country associations: PromptPay is paired with Thailand, whereas PayNow is paired with Singapore.

items.exam_note: Matching question: Thailand — PromptPay; do not confuse it with Singapore — PayNow.

terms.plain_meaning: इस table में Thailand की fast payment व्यवस्था का नाम

unpack.example_or_place: Thailand.
unpack.consequence: Completes the table's five distinct country-system associations.
unpack.visual_verb: Pair Thailand with PromptPay and contrast it with Singapore—PayNow.
unpack.level_extra: Similar payment-related names are not interchangeable country matches.

Notes explain scope, decisions with reasons, and source uncertainties.
No distinct teaching content is lost through consolidation; all named network examples are retained.
Meaning, rationale, examples and consequences are developed across the substantive items.
Explanations fit aspirants without introducing unnecessary technical architecture.
All substantive text and image-only content is captured.
No teachable content is dismissed as boilerplate.
All five table rows have separate items preserving both cells and their headers.
Every payment-flow box, arrow, direction and caption is identified.
₹1,000, ₹980 and MDR = 2% are preserved; symbols and the ₹20 calculation are explained.
Questions explain roles, mechanisms, qualifications and consequences at the required level.
Answer bases are appropriate and outside explanations are standard.
Content types suit the actual claims; the heading override is justified.
Prerequisites name concrete concepts such as percentages, card payments and international transfers.
Exam priorities and matching or correct-statement traps are sensible; no question links are fabricated.
No substantive native-text/image disagreement is evident; image-only content is separately captured.
The printed '&' is preserved and its intended 'and' reading explicitly supplied.
Book-derived answers and outside explanatory answers remain separate.
